tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

**IT IS BEAUTIFUL** — [ ] Kent has looked and nothing triggers the template veto · [x] no dialogs, spinners, hairball, colour-only meaning *(03)* · [x] keyboard end to end; reduced motion *(03)* · [ ] the visual checklist, cited by name, a *yes* on every line at three window sizes.

---

## Working rules (what changed on 2026-09-21)

- **One queue for heavy work** — `plans/scripts/heavy.sh`; its log is `plans/.heavy.log`. Agents run single test files, linters and type checks directly; a whole suite through the queue, at most twice. Playwright, repeat bars and anything paid: the coordinator only.
- **One agent per file-owning area; never two agents writing prose about one subject; never two pull requests open on one file.** `fixtures/hormuz.py` belongs to the engine lane; the Inspector, panel and tile to one browser agent at a time. Read-only analysts and reviewers in parallel are fine.
- **A read-only Opus review before every pull request — and one adversarial pass over every plan.** The first has found a must-fix on every branch of this stack; the second found ten in the first draft of this one.
- **A design that rests on a prototype opens with a spike and a kill criterion.**
- **How much browser testing a change needs — three tiers, not "20 cold runs".** (Kent asked on 2026-09-21 where the 20 came from: **nowhere in the committed repo** — no record, no chapter, no Makefile target; it was a coordinator's habit written only in these notes, grown out of five "flaky" tests that were real defects. Measured the same day: the 23-minute bar ran three times, ~70 minutes, and caught nothing one run plus CI would not have — the panel-wording mismatch failed 17 of 17; the layout race passed 20 of 20 locally and failed CI's first run.) **Tier 1 — every browser pull request:** ONE cold run of all end-to-end tests locally (~70 s) and the build, which is a second, slower, different machine on purpose. **Tier 2 — a change to timing-sensitive code** (canvas, layout, stream, growth, focus): tier 1, plus a NO-BROWSER test that injects the adverse timing (a late layout answer, a dropped size notification) — that is what pinned both real races of 2026-09-21, in milliseconds. **Tier 3 — a repeat bar only when a specific rare failure has been SEEN:** that one test, not the suite, sized to the rate (about 3k clean runs to be 95% sure a 1-in-k fault is gone). **Proposed to Kent, not yet accepted: a dated amendment to record 0008 saying this** (its "one end-to-end browser test" is also out of date — there are nine). **Not yet done, to make one run faster (68 s → ~25 s):** run the four replay tests in parallel workers; make the replay's pace a setting so tests run at ~150 ms an event instead of 600 (still paced — measure that the rectangle-before-claim moment survives); keep the late-layout-thread build as one permanent 20-second check.
- **Pay once.** Anything that moves the prompt fingerprint — or the request body the cassettes match on — is batched, recorded on the branch, and committed with the code. **Hormuz only until stack 05's freeze; then all four, once (R9).** `make eval` runs `ONLY=hormuz` until then.
- **Stacks two deep** *(Kent, R13 — in force; the dated amendment to record 0009 rides in the next docs pull request)*: a docs bottom and one code pull request on it; otherwise straight onto `main`, one at a time per lane.
- **Keep the evidence.** An analyst's scripts go in `plans/analysis/scripts/`, not a temp directory.
- **Spend:** about $27–29 of $500 on 2026-09-21; nothing spent in this session.

## 8. Lessons — read these twice

1. **After any interruption, check reality before acting.** `git log --oneline -5`, `git status`, `git worktree list`, `gh pr list`, and `STATUS.md`. Do not trust your memory of the repo; trust the repo.
2. **Append to `STATUS.md` before you stop**, and whenever the set of open pull requests or running agents changes. Record Kent's instructions there in his own words.
3. **Brief sub-agents fully, and point at the one copy.** They know only what you tell them. Give the plan and the decisions note by **absolute path in the main checkout** (readable from any worktree) rather than pasting tables — no transcription drift. Paste only what must be word for word on screen.
4. **Keep cross-references consistent.** After any rename or any changed number, search the whole repo. A fixture change in stack 03 made numbers stale in eight chapters, the PRD, a decision record and an end-to-end test.
5. **Whoever changes a fixture or an engine rule lists which chapter numbers went stale, and the sweep travels in the same pull request.** Resume the chapter's own writer for the sweep.
6. **Verify every sub-agent's claim yourself.** Run the tests and lints, read the diff against the owned-files list, hand-check arithmetic on a tiny map of your own, **launch the app and look**. A report is a hypothesis. In stack 03 this caught: a lint failure an agent reported as green, a plate overlap on a map the agent had not probed, and a fixed-height tile full of dead space.
7. **Write the shapes sheet before parallel writers start** — and for parallel stacks, the event or type vocabulary they share.
8. **Put a read-only reviewer over parallel writers, every time.** It found about ten blocking cross-chapter disagreements per stack — two names for one type, the same test named two ways, "six options" over a list of five, a block of invented numbers. Have it **re-do every worked number by hand from the fixture**.
9. **Two honest principles settle most small questions**: one rule over two (find the rule the code already obeys and name it once); and a code, a word or a number must mean what it says (that is why there is `edit_not_applicable`, why `killed` means only forced false, why the chip says "stated range · not computed").
10. **Never put a typed-in number where a computed one belongs — including in tests.** Assert directions, orderings and states; or compare a value with itself across a change.
11. **Property tests must build their inputs.** One that `assume()`s most inputs away fails Hypothesis's health check in CI on a bad seed while passing locally. CI is about 2.5× slower than this machine.
12. **The first pull request of a stack is small enough to write yourself**: commit chapter *stubs* (headings only) so code agents can branch off the spec branch at once.
13. **Opus agents can hit a session limit** ("resets 7am America/New_York"). If one dies, check disk state before reviving it by message.
15. **A client library accepting a shape proves nothing about the service.** In stack 04 the SDK built a schema from a union of three shapes without complaint and the service refused it on the first live call (`For 'anyOf', '$defs' is not supported`). Only a live call settles a vendor question — make the first one early, make it small, and do not close a chapter's open question on the library's say-so.
16. **Test a program as a program, and make a paid run impossible to lose.** Twice in stack 04 a run that cost money kept nothing: once because the recorder threw the receipt away with a file it would not write, once because the module's `__main__` guard sat above a function it called — invisible to every test (tests import, so everything is defined first) and to ruff and mypy. Run each `python -m` entry point in a subprocess test through its whole path; keep anything paid for incrementally, so a crash still leaves a file.
17. **A rare test failure is a bug until the evidence says otherwise.** Four times in stack 04 an agent's first instinct was "flaky — clear the example database": the keyboard left behind on a rebuilt tile; two keys in one frame; a locality leak through the day grid (a claim in a separate piece of the map moved by `.096`); a second through one global survival mask (`.083`). Every one was a real defect a user could hit. Find the falsifying input, rebuild it by hand, and decide with evidence whether the test or the product is wrong. And pytest TRUNCATES a repr — `Belief(p=1.85...` is `1.85e-05`, not a likelihood above 1.
18. **Several worktrees on one machine share one set of end-to-end ports.** Until stack 04 fixed it, `frontend/playwright.config.ts` used fixed ports and reused any server already up, so one agent's `npx playwright test` silently tested another branch's app — and "verified" numbers were wrong in both directions. Give every agent, and yourself, explicit ports (`KATALYST_E2E_BACKEND_PORT`, `KATALYST_E2E_FRONTEND_PORT`), never reuse a server, and never edit a source file under a running dev server (a hot reload blanks the page mid-test and looks like your change broke everything).
19. **One queue for heavy work, enforced by a script, not by asking.** Stack 04's first session ran three or four suites and 40× repeat bars at once; the load sat at 20–23 and the load itself caused failures that were then chased. `plans/scripts/heavy.sh` is a lock directory holding its owner's process id: whoever asks waits their turn. Agents run single test files, linters and type checks directly; a whole suite through the queue; playwright, repeat bars and anything paid are the coordinator's alone. Two 600-run bars and four agents' suites went through it on 2026-09-21 without one spurious failure.
20. **100% coverage and 259 green tests proved nothing about whether the arithmetic was right.** Three defects sat on the demo map — an observation that never reached a cause, endings deaf to half their causes, a supposition voided by a claim nobody believed — because no test compared the engine with an answer worked out independently, under an edit. Every engine needs an oracle that is *forbidden the engine's internals*, the way the locality oracle may not call `affected_set`. And check what an oracle can see: one that shares the core's tables proves the summing and is blind to a wrong table.
21. **Attack a plan before its owner sees it, and re-check a review before acting on it.** The two midpoint reviews read a `main` ten pull requests old: of one audit's blockers, six were already fixed, and one review's central claim about generation (the map is a tree) was false by measurement. Then the coordinator's own synthesis said "solved exactly" where an adversarial pass measured .12 of error, offered Kent a choice that was not optional, and under-counted the work by about 1.6×. One read-only red-team agent, told to break it, cost twenty minutes. A design that rests on a prototype opens with a spike and a kill criterion. And keep the evidence: an analyst's scripts go in `plans/analysis/scripts/`, not a temp directory.
22. **A green bar here is not a green bar there — and more runs of the same bar is not the answer.** On 2026-09-21 a replay test passed 20 cold runs of 20 on this machine and failed the build's FIRST run: the layout is worked out on its own thread, the build machine's thread was slower, and a claim took a rectangle's place at the origin. Throttling the processor did not reproduce it (that slows the page, not the layout thread); starting the layout thread 900 ms late did, at once. The same day a generated numbers file matched byte for byte across macOS/Arm and Linux/x86-64 — and its own margin test still went red on Linux, because with 280 numbers some value sits on a rounding boundary on some machine at ANY digit count. **Rules:** a test that reads a MOMENT (what stood when X arrived) gets a no-browser twin that injects the bad timing on purpose; a check that compares NUMBERS uses a stated tolerance, never text; and the amount of browser testing follows the three tiers in `PLAN.md`'s working rules — one cold run and the build by default, a repeat bar only for a rare failure that has actually been seen. The "20 cold runs" bar was never a recorded standard; it cost ~70 minutes that day and caught nothing one run plus the build would not have.
23. **The whole suite, through the queue, before EVERY push; and never edit a worktree while a bar is running in it.** Both broken once on 2026-09-21: a push after two test files let three stale health tests reach the build (#41's first run); an edit under a running bar hot-reloaded a fix into its dev server and voided three runs. Check `plans/.heavy.log` for an open START before touching a worktree.
14. **Say what you merged and why before Kent has to ask**, and if you take a step earlier than he literally asked (stack 03a was merged while 03b's last pull request was still being built), tell him plainly and offer to hold.

---

| Stack | What it proves | Plan |

1	This is a take home coding assignment for https://catalyst.app/.
2	
3	Catalyst is the agent layer for finance. We turn natural language — a thesis, strategy, hedge, or trading idea — into live execution across any market, venue, or asset class from prediction markets to commodities to tokens to private markets. It is a seed stage company with investments from Sequoia, Jump Trading, and Lux Capital.
4	
5	Here are more details about Catalyst: https://coastalhq.co/scoop/e3a34548-1964-4b30-96ea-52801a558dd2
6	
7	The goal of the project is to create a functional protoype of the concept behind Catalyst as a company. The full brief I was provided for this is located at ./ASSIGNMENT.md
8	
9	## Map
10	
11	| Where | What |
12	|-------|------|
13	| `PRODUCT_REQUIREMENTS.md` | The compressed seed: decisions, requirements, invariants, anti-patterns, roadmap as PR stacks |
14	| `ARCHITECTURE.md` | The technical counterpart: layers, data flow, where each invariant is enforced, runtime, testing. Living; marks each section built or planned |
15	| `docs/adr/` | Numbered decision records (MADR format: context, options, decision, consequences); `template.md`; `README.md` index. Higher number supersedes |
16	| `spec/` | The spec as a book: one directory per idea (`graph/`, `multiverse/`, `thesis/`, `generation/`, `workbench/`, `probes/`), each with a landing page; `vocabulary.md` is the shared language |
17	| `docs/research/` | Four independent research reports (2026-09-16) that fed the PRD; inputs, not decisions |
18	| `plans/` | **Local only, git-ignored.** Agent-to-agent handoffs, working notes, orchestration. Start at `plans/README.md`. Nothing here is a source of truth — anything durable moves into a root document, a decision record, or the spec |
19	| `docs/initial-brainstorming.md` | Kent's raw notes; the origin of trigger/sustain links and refinement |
20	| `backend/` | The Python server. `domain/` is the pure core — the rules of the map and the arithmetic that works a change through it, no network, no model, no clock — and it is property-tested against maps nobody wrote by hand. `engine/` builds a world from a map, a branch and a seed; `api/` serves it |
21	| `frontend/` | The browser app: the canvas that draws a map, the wires, the Inspector, the two-world overlay and the keyboard. It reads the stored example today and is not joined to the engine yet. `src/api/schema.ts` is generated from the server's own description of itself and is never edited by hand; `e2e/` holds the one end-to-end test |
22	
23	## Working agreements (interview, 2026-09-16)
24	
25	* **ADR-gated cadence.** An agent drafts the ADR and spec first; Kent accepts, rejects, or amends; only then is code written. Nothing is implemented against a `proposed` ADR. Decisions Kent has already taken are listed in `PRODUCT_REQUIREMENTS.md` §3 — do not re-litigate them.
26	* **Disgust veto.** Two conditions end a line of work immediately: a template-looking UI, and any state that cannot be traced to an input, a rule, or a cited source.
27	* **Vocabulary is the interface.** Use `spec/vocabulary.md` words exactly in docs, code, and UI copy.
28	* **Every number can say why.** Beliefs carry owner, interval, and provenance; two significant figures; model, user, and market beliefs are never merged.
29	* **Stacks tell the story.** One stack per spec; the bottom PR is docs-only; branch names are `<type>/<NN>-<slug>` with `NN` the stack number from the PRD roadmap. Conventional commits with `spec:` and `adr:` types in addition to the usual.
30	* **ARCHITECTURE.md is living.** A pull request that changes a boundary, layer, data flow, or runtime dependency updates it in the same PR.
31	* **Research reports are inputs.** Where a report and an ADR disagree, the ADR wins; where an ADR and the PRD disagree, fix the drift in the same PR.
32	
33	RULES FOR THIS REPO
34	
35	* Significant architectural decisions should be recorded at ./docs/adr in a numbered order. Higher number records supersede lower numbered ones.
36	* Enduring context between agents should live as all caps docs in the root of the repo, e.g. AGENTS.md, ASSIGNMENT.md, PRODUCT_REQUIREMENTS.md. These should always be kept up to date if you notice them drifting.
37	* More detailed descriptions, diagrams about particular systems or complex features should be written to ./spec
38	* Specs should follow best practices regarding spec-driven development. Some key aspects of specs for this repo should include invariants and anti-patterns
39	* This is an experimental prototype and I am a solo developer. However, I would like to use best practices regarding commit messages, PRs, and PR stacks to maintain the navigability, hygiene, and legibility of this repo.
40	* Docs should avoid jargon, reference to other docs, or unexplained abbreviations and symbols. They should be self-contained as much as possible. That is, explain in doc what the concepts being referenced are. This also extends to doc strings and comments in the code.

This is a take home coding assignment for https://catalyst.app/.

Catalyst is the agent layer for finance. We turn natural language — a thesis, strategy, hedge, or trading idea — into live execution across any market, venue, or asset class from prediction markets to commodities to tokens to private markets. It is a seed stage company with investments from Sequoia, Jump Trading, and Lux Capital.

Here are more details about Catalyst: https://coastalhq.co/scoop/e3a34548-1964-4b30-96ea-52801a558dd2

The goal of the project is to create a functional protoype of the concept behind Catalyst as a company. The full brief I was provided for this is located at ./ASSIGNMENT.md

## Map

| Where | What |
|-------|------|
| `PRODUCT_REQUIREMENTS.md` | The compressed seed: decisions, requirements, invariants, anti-patterns, roadmap as PR stacks |
| `ARCHITECTURE.md` | The technical counterpart: layers, data flow, where each invariant is enforced, runtime, testing. Living; marks each section built or planned |
| `docs/adr/` | Numbered decision records (MADR format: context, options, decision, consequences); `template.md`; `README.md` index. Higher number supersedes |
| `spec/` | The spec as a book: one directory per idea (`graph/`, `multiverse/`, `thesis/`, `generation/`, `workbench/`, `probes/`), each with a landing page; `vocabulary.md` is the shared language |
| `docs/research/` | Four independent research reports (2026-09-16) that fed the PRD; inputs, not decisions |
| `plans/` | **Local only, git-ignored.** Agent-to-agent handoffs, working notes, orchestration. Start at `plans/README.md`. Nothing here is a source of truth — anything durable moves into a root document, a decision record, or the spec |
| `docs/initial-brainstorming.md` | Kent's raw notes; the origin of trigger/sustain links and refinement |
| `backend/` | The Python server. `domain/` is the pure core — the rules of the map and the arithmetic that works a change through it, no network, no model, no clock — and it is property-tested against maps nobody wrote by hand. `engine/` builds a world from a map, a branch and a seed; `api/` serves it |
| `frontend/` | The browser app: the canvas that draws a map, the wires, the Inspector, the two-world overlay and the keyboard. It reads the stored example today and is not joined to the engine yet. `src/api/schema.ts` is generated from the server's own description of itself and is never edited by hand; `e2e/` holds the one end-to-end test |

## Working agreements (interview, 2026-09-16)

* **ADR-gated cadence.** An agent drafts the ADR and spec first; Kent accepts, rejects, or amends; only then is code written. Nothing is implemented against a `proposed` ADR. Decisions Kent has already taken are listed in `PRODUCT_REQUIREMENTS.md` §3 — do not re-litigate them.
* **Disgust veto.** Two conditions end a line of work immediately: a template-looking UI, and any state that cannot be traced to an input, a rule, or a cited source.
* **Vocabulary is the interface.** Use `spec/vocabulary.md` words exactly in docs, code, and UI copy.
* **Every number can say why.** Beliefs carry owner, interval, and provenance; two significant figures; model, user, and market beliefs are never merged.
* **Stacks tell the story.** One stack per spec; the bottom PR is docs-only; branch names are `<type>/<NN>-<slug>` with `NN` the stack number from the PRD roadmap. Conventional commits with `spec:` and `adr:` types in addition to the usual.
* **ARCHITECTURE.md is living.** A pull request that changes a boundary, layer, data flow, or runtime dependency updates it in the same PR.
* **Research reports are inputs.** Where a report and an ADR disagree, the ADR wins; where an ADR and the PRD disagree, fix the drift in the same PR.

RULES FOR THIS REPO

* Significant architectural decisions should be recorded at ./docs/adr in a numbered order. Higher number records supersede lower numbered ones.
* Enduring context between agents should live as all caps docs in the root of the repo, e.g. AGENTS.md, ASSIGNMENT.md, PRODUCT_REQUIREMENTS.md. These should always be kept up to date if you notice them drifting.
* More detailed descriptions, diagrams about particular systems or complex features should be written to ./spec
* Specs should follow best practices regarding spec-driven development. Some key aspects of specs for this repo should include invariants and anti-patterns
* This is an experimental prototype and I am a solo developer. However, I would like to use best practices regarding commit messages, PRs, and PR stacks to maintain the navigability, hygiene, and legibility of this repo.
* Docs should avoid jargon, reference to other docs, or unexplained abbreviations and symbols. They should be self-contained as much as possible. That is, explain in doc what the concepts being referenced are. This also extends to doc strings and comments in the code.
* Be concise, punchy, and succinct without sacrificing clarity. Use formatting as a communication and legibility aid.

13	# ADR-0008: Four test layers (five since the 2026-09-17 amendment); the LLM boundary is tested with committed cassettes and CI needs no API key
14	
15	## Context and Problem Statement
16	
17	The product's correctness claims are mathematical — an intervention touches only its descendants, edits compose, probabilities stay in bounds — while its inputs come from a language model and are never the same twice. Tests must prove the invariants in `PRODUCT_REQUIREMENTS.md` §9 over *generated* inputs, exercise the model boundary without spending money or leaking keys, and still let us measure prompt quality when we choose to. Where does each kind of test live, and what do we deliberately not test?
18	
19	## Decision Drivers
20	
21	* INV-3, INV-4, INV-5, INV-6, INV-7, INV-10 (assert versus observe, locality, patch replay, no loops, belief bounds, refinement adds back up) must be property-tested, not example-tested (NFR-3): thousands of generated inputs, with any failure shrunk to the smallest example that still breaks.
22	* INV-13: `ci.yml`, the continuous-integration workflow that runs on every push, passes with no `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`.
23	* NFR-8: a recorded response must never contain a key.
24	* D5(ii): a failing test must say *which invariant* broke.
25	* Solo developer: the suite must run in seconds locally.
26	
27	## Considered Options
28	
29	* A. **Four layers: pure-domain property tests · boundary tests backed by cassettes (recorded API responses replayed in tests) · an out-of-band eval harness · thin frontend tests**
30	* B. Hand-written stand-ins for the vendor's client library.
31	* C. Live API calls in continuous integration, behind a stored secret.
32	* D. No tests at the model boundary; test only the domain.
33	
34	## Decision Outcome
35	
36	Chosen option: "A", because it puts the weight where the claims are (the domain), makes the boundary deterministic and key-free, and keeps prompt quality measurable without making the shared build slow, costly, or flaky.
37	
38	**Layer 1 — pure domain (`backend/tests/unit/`).** The `hypothesis` library generates arbitrary valid graphs, branches, and intervention sequences. Named tests map to invariants:
39	
40	| Invariant | Test |
41	|---|---|
42	| INV-3 | `test_do_leaves_ancestors_unchanged`, `test_observe_may_update_ancestors` |
43	| INV-4 | `test_intervention_locality` — non-descendants byte-identical |
44	| INV-5 | `test_apply_empty_is_identity`, `test_patch_concat_equals_sequential_apply`, `test_world_replays_from_base_branch_seed` |
45	| INV-6 | `test_apply_preserves_dag`, `test_reflexive_links_have_positive_lag` |
46	| INV-7 | `test_belief_bounds_after_any_sequence` |
47	| INV-10 | `test_refine_marginalizes_to_parent` |
48	
49	`GraphEditMachine`, a `RuleBasedStateMachine` — a generated *sequence* of random interventions rather than one random input — re-checks INV-4, INV-6 and INV-7 after every step. Target: ≥85 % of `domain/` covered.
50	
51	**Layer 2 — model boundary (`backend/tests/boundary/`).** `pytest-recording` (a wrapper over vcrpy) saves each real HTTP exchange to a cassette file and replays it from then on. Tests carry `@pytest.mark.vcr`; the build runs `record_mode=none`, so an unrecorded call fails rather than dialling out; `filter_headers=["x-api-key", "authorization"]` strips credentials before anything is written; cassettes are committed under `backend/tests/cassettes/`. `scripts/record-cassettes.sh` re-records with `--record-mode=rewrite` against a real key. One cassette deliberately holds a proposal that would close a loop, and the test asserts the validator rejects it (`test_expand_rejects_cycle`) — fitting the schema is not the same as being a valid graph (ADR-0003, ADR-0006).
52	
53	**Layer 3 — evals (`evals/`).** `evals/cases/*.yaml` hold the four `ASSIGNMENT.md` examples. `make eval` runs live against `claude-opus-5` and asserts structure, never wording: no loops; at least one `market` or `not_tradeable` terminal (INV-9); `rationale` and `provenance` on every link; a source on every link marked `documented` (INV-2); resolution criteria on every proposition (INV-1); Verify cases return a graded path or an explicit `no_path` verdict (FR-7); non-zero `cache_read_input_tokens` on a run's second call, proving the prompt cache is hit. Results go to `evals/runs/<date>.tsv`. Not in the build.
54	
55	**Layer 5 — worked examples (`backend/tests/unit/fixtures/`, added by amendment 2026-09-17).** The stored example maps — today the Strait of Hormuz map and its strike branch — are tested as data: each validates clean, exercises every shape the rules layer defines, and survives the trip to the browser. They are example tests, not property tests, and they are the golden inputs the engine and canvas stacks build on.
56	
57	**Layer 4 — frontend.** vitest with Testing Library for the layout-pinning logic, the diff-state reducer, and the intervention-panel reducer. One end-to-end browser test (ADR-0007 Confirmation).
58	
59	**Deliberately skipped in v1:** a model grading narrative quality; image snapshot comparisons; contract tests between services; load tests; mutation testing (breaking code on purpose to see whether tests notice); more than one end-to-end test; coverage thresholds outside `domain/`.
60	
61	### Consequences
62	
63	* Good, because a reviewer can run the whole suite with no key in under a minute and read the invariant names as the test list.
64	* Good, because prompt changes have a regression harness (`make eval`) whose cost we choose when to pay.
65	* Bad, because cassettes drift when prompts change; re-recording is a scripted, documented step, and any pull request that changes a prompt must re-record.
66	* Bad, because evals are non-deterministic; we assert structure, not exact output, and keep them out of the build so flakiness never blocks a merge.
67	* Neutral, because `api/` and `engine/` orchestration are lightly tested by design; the README says so.
68	
69	### Confirmation
70	
71	* Continuous-integration job `backend`: `uv sync --frozen` (install the exact pinned dependencies) → `ruff check` and `ruff format --check` (lint and formatting) → `mypy --strict src/katalyst/domain` (type check) → `pytest --record-mode=none`. The job has no `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` in its environment (INV-13); a test that needs one fails loudly, because vcrpy raises `CannotOverwriteExistingCassetteException` rather than making a live call.
72	* `gitleaks`, a secret scanner, runs before every commit and scans the cassettes.
73	* Pull-request template item: "prompt changed? cassettes re-recorded, `make eval` scorecard attached".
74	
75	## Pros and Cons of the Options
76	
77	### A. Four layers (chosen)
78	
79	* Good, because the build is deterministic, cassettes carry real HTTP shapes, and invariants are checked over generated inputs.
80	* Bad, because two libraries to learn (vcrpy, hypothesis); both are mature.
81	
82	### B. Hand-written stand-ins
83	
84	* Good, because no cassette files.
85	* Bad, because a stand-in encodes our assumptions about the client library rather than its behaviour; it rots silently and never catches a real change of shape.
86	
87	### C. Live API in continuous integration
88	
89	* Good, because always current.
90	* Bad, because non-deterministic, costs money on every push, needs a secret in the build, and breaks INV-13.
91	
92	### D. No boundary tests
93	
94	* Bad, because the rejection path — loops, missing criteria — is exactly where the product's honesty lives.
95	
96	## More Information
97	
98	* Interview D5(ii) (traceability), D9 (decision-gated cadence — invariants are named before code).
99	* `docs/research/04-engineering-structure.md` §4 (testing layers) and §6 (invariants phrased as claims true for every input, each with a named generation strategy).
100	* pytest-recording: https://github.com/kiwicom/pytest-recording · hypothesis: https://hypothesis.readthedocs.io/
101	
102	## Amendment (2026-09-17)
103	
104	Stack 02 added a fifth kind of test that the four layers above did not name: the worked-example tests under `backend/tests/unit/fixtures/`, which check the stored example maps as data. Layer 5 above describes it. The four original layers, the cassette rules, and the keyless build are unchanged. Amended in place at Kent's request rather than superseded, because nothing in the decision changed — one layer was missing from the list.
105

1	/**
2	 * How the one end-to-end test runs.
3	 *
4	 * There is exactly one, and it drives the real app in a real browser against
5	 * the real server. Everything else about this product is checked by tests that
6	 * need neither — the rules of the map in the server's own suite, the components
7	 * in a simulated page. This one exists for the thing neither can check: that the
8	 * two halves, started as a person would start them, actually draw the stored
9	 * example.
10	 *
11	 * **Both halves are started here rather than by hand**, so that running it is
12	 * one command and so that the build job is the same command. The server is
13	 * started on a port of its own and the browser app is told where to find it, the
14	 * same way the packaged app is told.
15	 *
16	 * **No model key, anywhere.** The screen this test drives is fed by
17	 * `GET /api/fixtures/hormuz`, which is a stored example: it calls no model and
18	 * needs no key. The whole suite passes with nothing configured, which is the
19	 * rule the build is held to, and the environment below is written out in full so
20	 * that nothing is inherited by accident.
21	 */
22	
23	import { defineConfig, devices } from "@playwright/test";
24	import { assertPortsAreFree, BACKEND_PORT, FRONTEND_PORT } from "./e2e/ports.js";
25	
26	/**
27	 * **Both ports come from the environment, and nothing is ever reused.**
28	 *
29	 * Several worktrees of this repository are often open on one machine and every
30	 * one of them wants these two numbers. Playwright's `reuseExistingServer` is
31	 * worse than a collision: it attaches to whatever is answering, so a run in one
32	 * worktree tests the branch checked out in another and reports it green. That
33	 * has happened here, in both directions, and neither side could tell from the
34	 * output. So the defaults are the numbers continuous integration has always
35	 * used, `KATALYST_E2E_BACKEND_PORT` and `KATALYST_E2E_FRONTEND_PORT` override
36	 * them, and `e2e/ports.ts` stops the run before the first test if either is
37	 * taken — naming the port and the variable that moves it.
38	 */
39	const SERVER_PORT = BACKEND_PORT;
40	const APP_PORT = FRONTEND_PORT;
41	
42	// Asked before anything is started, because nothing later is early enough.
43	assertPortsAreFree();
44	
45	export default defineConfig({
46	  testDir: "./e2e",
47	  // One test, run once. A retry would hide a flake, and a flake in a test that
48	  // drives two servers is a fault worth seeing.
49	  retries: 0,
50	  // Long enough for the layout engine's background thread to answer twice —
51	  // once for the map and once for the branch — on a slow build machine.
52	  timeout: 60_000,
53	  expect: { timeout: 15_000 },
54	  reporter: [["list"]],
55	  use: {
56	    baseURL: `http://localhost:${APP_PORT}`,
57	    // The window the whole interface is designed against. Every measurement in
58	    // the visual review was taken at this size.
59	    viewport: { width: 1600, height: 1000 },
60	    trace: "off",
61	  },
62	  projects: [
63	    {
64	      name: "chromium",
65	      // The window last, on purpose: the device preset carries one of its own,
66	      // and the whole interface was measured against this one.
67	      use: { ...devices["Desktop Chrome"], viewport: { width: 1600, height: 1000 } },
68	    },
69	  ],
70	  webServer: [
71	    {
72	      // The Python half, from its own directory, with the two keys it might have
73	      // inherited explicitly unset. It needs neither: the stored example is a
74	      // file on disk.
75	      command: `uv run uvicorn katalyst.api.main:app --port ${SERVER_PORT}`,
76	      cwd: "../backend",
77	      url: `http://localhost:${SERVER_PORT}/api/healthz`,
78	      // Never reused. A run that attaches to somebody else's server tests
79	      // somebody else's branch and says it was yours.
80	      reuseExistingServer: false,
81	      timeout: 120_000,
82	      env: {
83	        ANTHROPIC_API_KEY: "",
84	        FRED_API_KEY: "",
85	        // **The replay's pacing is left on, and that is deliberate.**
86	        //
87	        // `KATALYST_REPLAY_INSTANT` exists so a test need not wait out a delay
88	        // that is there for a reviewer's benefit, and for most tests it would be
89	        // free. It is not free here: `generate.spec.ts`'s whole subject is a map
90	        // *arriving* — a rectangle standing before any claim, the growing edge
91	        // moving, the chips resolving last and once — and with the pacing off
92	        // every event lands in one tick, React folds them into one render, and
93	        // the screen goes straight from nothing to a finished map. There is then
94	        // no moment at which the thing being tested is true, and the test fails
95	        // saying it could not find a rectangle. Turning the pacing off to make a
96	        // test faster would be turning off the behaviour the test is for.
97	        //
98	        // It costs seconds: the whole suite runs in about twenty.
99	      },
100	    },
101	    {
102	      // The browser half, told where the server is exactly as the packaged app
103	      // is told.
104	      command: `npm run dev -- --port ${APP_PORT} --strictPort`,
105	      url: `http://localhost:${APP_PORT}/`,
106	      reuseExistingServer: false,
107	      timeout: 120_000,
108	      env: { KATALYST_API_URL: `http://localhost:${SERVER_PORT}` },
109	    },
110	  ],
111	});

1	import { expect, type Locator, type Page } from "@playwright/test";
2	
3	/**
4	 * Waiting, and why every read in a browser test goes through it.
5	 *
6	 * **Nothing here reads a value the page has not settled on.** These tests drive
7	 * two servers, a background layout thread and a drawing library that measures
8	 * its own boxes, so at any moment the screen may be showing the answer to the
9	 * question before last. Every read goes through one of the helpers below, and
10	 * each of them waits for a *named* signal rather than for a number of
11	 * milliseconds — a sleep is a guess, and the build machine is about two and a
12	 * half times slower than the machine it was guessed on.
13	 *
14	 * They live in a file of their own because both browser tests need them, and a
15	 * helper copied into a second file is a second helper: the day one of these
16	 * learns about a new way the screen can lie, only one test would learn it.
17	 */
18	
19	/**
20	 * Wait until the map has been laid out, with every tile in a place of its own.
21	 *
22	 * Where the tiles go is worked out on a background thread, so for a moment after
23	 * the map appears the tiles are still stacked. Waiting for **every** tile to be
24	 * somewhere different is the honest signal, and it is the one that survives a
25	 * second layout: after a branch opens the tiles are already spread out from the
26	 * layout before it, so "more than one place" is satisfied before the new answer
27	 * has landed and says nothing at all.
28	 *
29	 * @param page The page the map is on.
30	 * @param tiles How many tiles this map has. A layered layout gives every tile a
31	 *   place of its own — two tiles on one spot is the collision the layout exists
32	 *   to prevent — so the count of places is the count of tiles exactly when the
33	 *   layout has landed.
34	 */
35	export async function waitForTheLayout(page: Page, tiles: number): Promise<void> {
36	  await expect(page.locator(".react-flow__node")).toHaveCount(tiles);
37	  await expect
38	    .poll(
39	      () =>
40	        page
41	          .locator(".react-flow__node")
42	          .evaluateAll(
43	            (nodes) => new Set(nodes.map((node) => (node as HTMLElement).style.transform)).size,
44	          ),
45	      { timeout: 30_000, message: "the map was never laid out" },
46	    )
47	    .toBe(tiles);
48	  await expect(page.locator(".react-flow__node").first()).toBeVisible();
49	}
50	
51	/**
52	 * Read one value off the screen, once the screen has settled on it.
53	 *
54	 * The shape is not decoration: it is what "settled" means here. A chip holds an
55	 * absence, then a number; waiting for the number's shape is waiting for the
56	 * engine. And the read itself is `textContent` rather than `innerText`, which
57	 * is empty until the drawing library has measured the tile.
58	 *
59	 * @param where The one element the value is in.
60	 * @param shape What the value looks like once it is there.
61	 */
62	export async function readWhenReady(where: Locator, shape: RegExp): Promise<string> {
63	  await expect(where).toBeVisible();
64	  await expect(where).toHaveText(shape);
65	  return ((await where.textContent()) ?? "").trim();
66	}
67	
68	/**
69	 * Wait until the engine has answered for this branch and the map has been laid
70	 * out again.
71	 *
72	 * The line under the map names the branch it folded on, and it is written from
73	 * the world the engine handed back — so it is there exactly when that world is.
74	 *
75	 * @param page The page the map is on.
76	 * @param branch The branch's name, as the reader typed it.
77	 * @param tiles How many tiles the map has with this branch folded on.
78	 */
79	export async function waitForTheBranch(page: Page, branch: string, tiles: number): Promise<void> {
80	  await expect(page.locator(".map-bar__where")).toContainText(branch);
81	  await expect(page.locator(".map-origin")).toContainText(`the branch "${branch}" folded onto it`);
82	  await waitForTheLayout(page, tiles);
83	}
84	
85	/**
86	 * Wait until the map has said, out loud, what this edit did.
87	 *
88	 * This is the signal an edit is finished. The counts in the sentence are the
89	 * engine's own, one per claim it called shifted, so the sentence cannot be there
90	 * until the difference is — and it is a *different* sentence from the one before
91	 * the edit, which is what makes waiting for it waiting rather than passing.
92	 *
93	 * @param page The page the map is on.
94	 * @param sentence The whole line, word for word.
95	 */
96	export async function waitForTheAnswer(page: Page, sentence: string): Promise<void> {
97	  await expect(page.locator(".map-live")).toHaveText(sentence);
98	}
99	
100	/**
101	 * Wait until the map has stopped moving, and say where it came to rest.
102	 *
103	 * Framing the map is an animation, so the transform is read twice and believed
104	 * only when the two agree. What it is for is the claim that flipping between the
105	 * two worlds moves nothing: a transform read mid-frame would make that claim
106	 * about two different moments.
107	 */
108	export async function whereTheMapCameToRest(page: Page): Promise<string> {
109	  const viewport = page.locator(".react-flow__viewport");
110	  let last = "";
111	  await expect
112	    .poll(
113	      async () => {
114	        const now = (await viewport.getAttribute("style")) ?? "";
115	        const settled = now !== "" && now === last;
116	        last = now;
117	        return settled;
118	      },
119	      { timeout: 30_000, message: "the map never stopped moving" },
120	    )
121	    .toBe(true);
122	  return last;
123	}
124	
125	/** Which claim the keyboard is standing on, or nothing when it is off the map. */
126	export function standingOn(page: Page): Promise<string | undefined> {
127	  return page.evaluate(
128	    () => document.activeElement?.closest<HTMLElement>(".react-flow__node")?.dataset.id,
129	  );
130	}
131	
132	/**
133	 * Put the keyboard on one claim's tile, the way a reader would, and wait until
134	 * it is there.
135	 *
136	 * **A map key only works when the keyboard is on the map**, and that is the
137	 * product's rule rather than this test's convenience: Space belongs to whatever
138	 * button the keyboard is on, so `useMapKeys` hands it over when there is one and
139	 * flips the two worlds only when there is not. Where focus happens to be after
140	 * a command has run is not something a test may assume — under load it is
141	 * sometimes a button, and then the keystroke is correctly ignored and the test
142	 * fails for a reason that is not a fault.
143	 *
144	 * @param page The page the map is on.
145	 * @param claim The claim whose tile the keyboard should stand on.
146	 */
147	export async function standOn(page: Page, claim: string): Promise<void> {
148	  await expect
149	    .poll(
150	      async () => {
151	        // The focusing is inside the poll, not before it. A re-render replaces
152	        // the tile's element and the keyboard falls back to the page, so asking
153	        // again and again whether it landed would ask for ever; what has to be
154	        // retried is the standing, not the looking.
155	        await page.locator(`.react-flow__node[data-id="${claim}"]`).focus();
156	        return await standingOn(page);
157	      },
158	      { timeout: 15_000, message: `the keyboard never stood on ${claim}` },
159	    )
160	    .toBe(claim);
161	}
162	
163	/**
164	 * Where one tile sits, once the drawing library has put it somewhere.
165	 *
166	 * **The place, and nothing else about the element.** The library writes several
167	 * things into a tile's style — its stacking order, whether the pointer may reach
168	 * it, and whether it is visible at all, which it turns off and on again as it
169	 * measures boxes — and only one of them is where the tile is. Comparing the
170	 * whole style across a change compares those too, and then "nothing already
171	 * placed moved" fails on a tile that was merely being re-measured. For the same
172	 * reason this waits for the tile to have a **place** rather than for it to be
173	 * visible: where it sits is a fact about the layout, and whether it is painted
174	 * this instant is not.
175	 *
176	 * @param tile The tile's element on the map.
177	 */
178	export async function whereTheTileSits(tile: Locator): Promise<string> {
179	  await expect(tile).toHaveCount(1);
180	  await expect
181	    .poll(
182	      async () => /translate\([^)]*\)/.exec((await tile.getAttribute("style")) ?? "")?.[0] ?? "",
183	      { timeout: 30_000, message: "the tile was never placed" },
184	    )
185	    .not.toBe("");
186	  return /translate\([^)]*\)/.exec((await tile.getAttribute("style")) ?? "")?.[0] ?? "";
187	}
188

1	/**
2	 * The two ports the end-to-end run uses, and the check that they are free.
3	 *
4	 * **Several worktrees of this repository are often open on one machine**, and
5	 * every one of them wants to start a server and a browser app. They cannot all
6	 * have the same two numbers. Playwright's own answer — `reuseExistingServer` —
7	 * is worse than a collision: it quietly attaches to whatever happens to be
8	 * answering on that port, so a run in one worktree tests the branch checked out
9	 * in another and reports it as green. That has already happened here, in both
10	 * directions, and neither side could tell from the output.
11	 *
12	 * So: the ports come from the environment, they default to the numbers
13	 * continuous integration has always used, nothing is ever reused, and a port
14	 * that is taken stops the run **before anything is started**, with a sentence
15	 * that says which port and what to do about it.
16	 *
17	 * **The check is made when the configuration is read**, which is the only
18	 * moment early enough. Playwright starts its servers before it runs anything
19	 * else it offers, and its own message for a taken port ends by suggesting
20	 * `reuseExistingServer: true` — which is the fault, recommended as the cure.
21	 * Being first is the whole point, so the check is synchronous, which asking a
22	 * socket is not: it is made in a child process that does the asking and exits
23	 * with the answer.
24	 */
25	
26	import { execFileSync } from "node:child_process";
27	
28	/** Where the Python half answers during a run. */
29	export const BACKEND_PORT = Number(process.env.KATALYST_E2E_BACKEND_PORT ?? 8015);
30	
31	/** Where the browser app is served during a run. */
32	export const FRONTEND_PORT = Number(process.env.KATALYST_E2E_FRONTEND_PORT ?? 5187);
33	
34	/**
35	 * Can this machine still open that port?
36	 *
37	 * By asking for it and letting it go, which is the only answer that is about
38	 * the port rather than about what somebody believes is running. A machine that
39	 * will not run the check at all is given the benefit of the doubt: Playwright
40	 * still refuses to start on a taken port, and a check that cannot run must not
41	 * be a check that fails.
42	 *
43	 * @param port The port to try.
44	 */
45	function free(port: number): boolean {
46	  const asking =
47	    "const s=require('node:net').createServer();" +
48	    "s.once('error',()=>process.exit(1));" +
49	    `s.once('listening',()=>s.close(()=>process.exit(0)));s.listen(${port},'127.0.0.1');`;
50	  try {
51	    execFileSync(process.execPath, ["-e", asking], { stdio: "ignore" });
52	    return true;
53	  } catch (whatever) {
54	    return (whatever as { status?: number }).status !== 1;
55	  }
56	}
57	
58	/**
59	 * Stop, before anything is started, if either port is taken.
60	 *
61	 * The sentence names the port, names the thing that is probably holding it, and
62	 * gives the one line that fixes it — because the person reading it is usually
63	 * somebody who did not know another worktree was running at all.
64	 */
65	export function assertPortsAreFree(): void {
66	  // **Only in the process that starts the servers.** Playwright reads this
67	  // configuration again in every worker it forks, and by then the ports are in
68	  // use — by the very servers it started, which is the one case that is not a
69	  // collision. A worker names itself in the environment; the first process does
70	  // not.
71	  if (process.env.TEST_WORKER_INDEX !== undefined) {
72	    return;
73	  }
74	  for (const [port, half, variable] of [
75	    [BACKEND_PORT, "the server", "KATALYST_E2E_BACKEND_PORT"],
76	    [FRONTEND_PORT, "the browser app", "KATALYST_E2E_FRONTEND_PORT"],
77	  ] as const) {
78	    if (free(port)) {
79	      continue;
80	    }
81	    throw new Error(
82	      `\n\nPort ${port}, where ${half} would be started, is already in use — most likely ` +
83	        `another worktree of this repository running its own end-to-end tests.\n\n` +
84	        `Nothing is reused here on purpose: a run that attached to it would test whichever ` +
85	        `branch that is and call the result yours.\n\n` +
86	        `Stop the other run, or give this one a port of its own:\n\n` +
87	        `    ${variable}=${port + 40} npm run e2e\n`,
88	    );
89	  }
90	}

"""The one place environment variables are read.

Why one place
-------------
If any module could reach for an environment variable, no one could say what the
program reads or what it does when something is missing. Here the answer is one
small class: the names it reads are its field names, and the default for each is
written next to it. Everywhere else asks `get_settings()`.

The field names are spelled in capitals on purpose, so that the name in the code
and the name in the environment are the same string. There is no rule to learn.

Both keys are optional while the program starts. A missing key is not a crash; it
is a fact `/api/readyz` reports, so the first screen can say plainly what works
and what does not.
"""

from functools import lru_cache
from typing import Literal

from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings, SettingsConfigDict


class Settings(BaseSettings):
    """Everything this program reads from its environment.

    Attributes:
        ANTHROPIC_API_KEY: The key for the language model that proposes
            propositions and links. First needed in stack 04, which generates a
            map from a sentence. Until then the program runs without it, and
            the tests run without it forever: they replay recorded answers.
        FRED_API_KEY: The key for the Federal Reserve Economic Data service, a
            public source of economic time series. First needed in stack 05,
            where a proposition can be grounded in a published series.
        KATALYST_MODEL: Which model the pipeline asks. One setting, read once, and
            nothing outside `engine/client.py` and `engine/pricing.py` knows
            which it is. The default is the cheaper of the two while the shape of
            the thing is still being worked out; the more capable one is one
            setting away for a final recording.
        KATALYST_EFFORT: How hard the model tries, pinned for a whole run and
            never varied between calls — varying it would throw away the
            remembered prefix the run is reading back cheaply. Left empty, the
            service's own default applies and the setting is not sent at all.
        KATALYST_RECORDINGS: Where the committed recordings are read from. Left
            empty, `backend/recordings/`. A test or an end-to-end browser run
            points it at a folder of its own.
        KATALYST_RUNS: Where every paid run is written, whatever becomes of it.
            Left empty, `backend/.runs/`. A test that starts the recorder as a
            program points it somewhere throwaway, because that folder holds what
            real money bought and nothing may overwrite it.
        KATALYST_ANSWERER: The import path of a factory that builds the answerer,
            as `module:name`. Left empty — which it is everywhere but a test — the
            live answerer is built from the key. It exists so that the recorder
            can be run **as a program**, end to end, with no key and no network:
            two paid runs have been lost to bugs that only exist when a module is
            started rather than imported. A run answered this way is never written
            as a recording, whatever else it produces.
        KATALYST_REPLAY_INSTANT: Whether a recorded generation plays back with no pause
            between its events. Off by default, because the pause is what makes a
            replay read as a map arriving rather than appearing. The test suite
            and the build's own check turn it on; it is deliberately not
            something a request can ask for, since a client that could skip the
            pacing could skip the thing a recording exists to show.
    """

    model_config = SettingsConfigDict(
        # A local `.env` file is read when present. It is never committed.
        env_file=".env",
        env_file_encoding="utf-8",
        # Unrelated environment variables are ignored rather than rejected.
        extra="ignore",
        # Field names match environment-variable names exactly.
        case_sensitive=True,
    )

    ANTHROPIC_API_KEY: str | None = None
    FRED_API_KEY: str | None = None
    KATALYST_MODEL: str = "claude-sonnet-5"
    KATALYST_EFFORT: Literal["low", "medium", "high", "xhigh", "max", ""] = ""
    KATALYST_RECORDINGS: str = ""
    KATALYST_RUNS: str = ""
    KATALYST_ANSWERER: str = ""
    KATALYST_REPLAY_INSTANT: bool = False


@lru_cache
def get_settings() -> Settings:
    """Return the settings, reading the environment only on the first call.

    The answer is cached so that the environment is read once per process and
    every caller sees the same values. A test that needs different values does
    not edit the environment: it replaces this function, either through the web
    framework's dependency override or by clearing the cache with
    `get_settings.cache_clear()`.

    Returns:
        The settings for this process.
    """
    return Settings()

if recording is None:
        # A receipt comes before every ending, this one included: the grammar
        # puts it second to last in **both** endings, and a receipt of zeroes is
        # the truth here. A stream with no receipt at all says nothing, and a
        # reader cannot tell it from one that forgot (2026-09-20).
        yield _nothing_spent(time.monotonic() - started)
        yield Failed(
            message=(
                "This copy of Katalyst has no model key and no recording of that "
                "sentence, so there is nothing it can honestly show you. The examples "
                "it can replay are listed on the first screen."
            )
        )
        return

    # **One identifier per viewing, minted here.** The recording's own is a
    # constant in a committed file, so two people opening the same card shared
    # one entry in the store and overwrote each other's working — and whichever
    # finished last decided what both of them read afterwards (2026-09-20). The
    # recording's own identifier is kept as a field, because it is what says
    # which file this was.
    announced = mint_id()
    played_from = next(
        (
            payload["generation_id"]
            for name, payload in recording.lines
            if name == events.NAMES[GenerationStarted]
        ),
        recording.header.base_id,
    )
    working = Transcript(
        generation_id=announced,
        played_from=played_from,
        hypothesis=recording.hypothesis,
        # A Verify recording knows where it was asked to get to, and the
        # transcript used to say it had no destination at all (2026-09-20).
        target=recording.target,
        seed=recording.header.seed,
        on=recording.header.recording_date,
        mode="replay",
    )
    at = 0
    worked_through = False
    graph = None
    try:

        # playing it is, so it sits inside the same guard.
        # The reader's own likelihood is an **input**, not part of the
        # recording, so it is stamped here exactly as the live path stamps it.
        # It was accepted by the route and then dropped in silence on this path

1	/**
2	 * Which boxes the map draws, and where.
3	 *
4	 * The layout runs on a background thread and **answers later**, so at every
5	 * moment a map is growing there are boxes nobody has found a place for yet. This
6	 * file is the one answer to what happens to them, written apart from the canvas
7	 * so that it can be read, and checked, without a browser.
8	 *
9	 * On this machine the window is shorter than a frame and nobody ever sees it. On
10	 * a slower one it is long enough to read, and what is drawn in it is the whole of
11	 * what this file is about.
12	 */
13	
14	import type { Position } from "./elkGraph";
15	import type { MapNode } from "./toFlow";
16	
17	/** Where the map starts. The only place this file ever puts a box itself. */
18	export const THE_ORIGIN: Position = { x: 0, y: 0 };
19	
20	/** One box, and the place it is drawn at. */
21	export type PlacedBox = MapNode & { position: Position };
22	
23	/** What the map has on the glass. */
24	export interface OnTheGlass {
25	  /** Every box that is drawn, each with the place it is drawn at. */
26	  readonly boxes: readonly PlacedBox[];
27	  /**
28	   * The reserved rectangles among them, with their places.
29	   *
30	   * Handed back so that the next answer can be worked out from this one: a
31	   * rectangle comes down when the claim it was holding a place for is drawn, and
32	   * that cannot be decided without knowing which rectangles were standing.
33	   */
34	  readonly rectangles: readonly PlacedBox[];
35	}
36	
37	/** Is this box a reserved rectangle rather than a claim? */
38	function isRectangle(box: MapNode): boolean {
39	  return box.type === "skeleton";
40	}
41	
42	/**
43	 * Work out what the map draws.
44	 *
45	 * Three rules, which are one rule seen from three sides: **the map draws a box
46	 * where the layout put it, and a reserved rectangle keeps saying where the next
47	 * claim goes until that claim is drawn.**
48	 *
49	 * **A box is drawn where the layout put it, and nowhere else.** A box the layout
50	 * has not placed has no place, and drawing it at the map's origin gives it one
51	 * the layout never agreed to — so it appears at the origin and then hops to
52	 * wherever the layout actually wanted it, on the one screen whose whole promise
53	 * is that nothing already drawn ever moves (INV-workbench.64).
54	 *
55	 * **A reserved rectangle stands until the claim it was holding a place for is on
56	 * the glass** — not until the event carrying that claim arrived. Those are
57	 * different moments, and everything between them is a map with a claim on its
58	 * way and no rectangle anywhere: a growing map that has stopped saying where it
59	 * is going. It is not a corner case. A generated map's frontier is usually one
60	 * claim wide, so it turns over completely every few proposals, and each turnover
61	 * is one of these moments. The rectangle goes the instant the map is whole
62	 * again, and a rectangle whose claim closed with nothing coming after it — a
63	 * third refusal, a broken run, the likelihoods landing — goes at once, because
64	 * then nothing on the map is waiting for a place.
65	 *
66	 * **And before the layout has answered anything at all, the map holds the first
67	 * rectangle at the origin itself.** The origin is nobody's place then: there is
68	 * nothing to be drawn on top of, and a generation's first paint may not be an
69	 * empty stage (INV-workbench.61 — a rectangle carrying the reader's own sentence
70	 * is on screen before the first proposal comes back). The box that takes it is a
71	 * rectangle and never a claim.
72	 *
73	 * @param boxes Every box the map holds, in reading order.
74	 * @param places Where the layout has said each box goes. Empty until it answers.
75	 * @param standing The rectangles this returned last time it was asked, so the
76	 *   ones still holding a place can go on holding it.
77	 */
78	export function whatIsOnTheGlass(
79	  boxes: readonly MapNode[],
80	  places: ReadonlyMap<string, Position>,
81	  standing: readonly PlacedBox[],
82	): OnTheGlass {
83	  const drawn: PlacedBox[] = [];
84	  let somethingHasNowhereToGo = false;
85	  for (const box of boxes) {
86	    const at = places.get(box.id);
87	    if (at === undefined) {
88	      somethingHasNowhereToGo = true;
89	      continue;
90	    }
91	    drawn.push({ ...box, position: at });
92	  }
93	  if (!somethingHasNowhereToGo) {
94	    return { boxes: drawn, rectangles: drawn.filter(isRectangle) };
95	  }
96	
97	  // Something on the map is waiting for a place, so every rectangle that was
98	  // standing goes on standing: each of them is holding the place of a claim that
99	  // is on its way and not yet drawn. They were placed in the arrangement that is
100	  // still on the glass, so none of them can land on anything.
101	  const alreadyDrawn = new Set(drawn.map((box) => box.id));
102	  const held = standing.filter((box) => !alreadyDrawn.has(box.id));
103	
104	  // Nothing has ever been placed, and nothing is being held. This is a
105	  // generation's first paint: the map puts its own first rectangle at the origin
106	  // rather than show an empty stage. A map with no rectangles at all — every
107	  // finished map — waits, because it has nothing to say yet and no reason to
108	  // guess where it would go.
109	  const first =
110	    drawn.length === 0 && held.length === 0
111	      ? boxes
112	          .filter(isRectangle)
113	          .slice(0, 1)
114	          .map((box) => ({ ...box, position: THE_ORIGIN }))
115	      : [];
116	
117	  const all = [...drawn, ...held, ...first];
118	  return { boxes: all, rectangles: all.filter(isRectangle) };
119	}

Skeleton tiles, claims, wires in causal order, refusals in the strip beside the map, skeletons coming down as each growth event's `frontier` shrinks — the canvas cannot tell, and that is the point.
171:`POST /api/generate/insert` arrives. With no key, the route compares the sentence against the header's `RecordedInsert.claim_in_words`, **matched on the exact words after trimming surrounding spaces**, and hands back the `Insert` recorded against it — a claim and its arrows, drafted live when the recording was made and validated then exactly as it would be now.
195:* **A kept run carries more than a recording does, and it is written twice** (*decided here*, 2026-09-20; the chapter first said the two were the same file format). 248:It is a setting for one reason that is not configurability: **the tests and the browser's end-to-end run need to point at a small recording of their own.** The end-to-end test drives the real launchpad through the real stream with no key, and it should not depend on whichever of the four real recordings happens to be committed today, nor take a real recording's minute of paced playback. One setting gives it a fixture-sized file of its own, through exactly the same code path. Without it the choice is a test that is slow and coupled to real recordings, or a second loading path built only for tests — and a second path is the one that rots.
265:Kent settled this on 2026-09-17 (G6), and it is an order chosen to spend the least money on a prompt that is still moving:

323:3. **One recorded intervention per example, or two?** One is enough to prove the mechanism and it is what record 0012 settled. A second — an insert that the validator *refuses* — would show the reviewer the rejection path on an intervention as well as on a proposal, for the price of one more drafted claim per recording. Worth asking once the cost of a recording is measured.
324:4. **Whether a recording should carry the wall-clock gaps of the run that made it**, so pacing could follow the real rhythm — a fast proposal, then a slow one that searched — instead of a fixed delay. It would read more like the live product and cost four numbers per file.
